old: Candidate restriction can reduce influence-maximization search costs, yet its apparent quality depends on a reference solution that is itself estimated. A measured gain or loss may reflect reference sampling, numerical changes in candidate eligibility, or both. We use paired selection and independent spread evaluation to distinguish these effects by varying reference budget and ranking precision separately. Evidence comes from a small, selected sample of real-world networks: three external topologies, with four small contact graphs providing separate controls. On ca-GrQc, increasing the reference budget changes mean incremental spread from a 5.61\% gain to a 5.07\% loss. This reversal disappears in a post-hoc control that tightens PageRank tolerance. Budget-dependent seed changes persist, and reference-set changes have different utility consequences. Across the external networks, degree-based pools reproduce all 15 highest-budget reference trajectories, whereas PageRank losses persist on the two directed networks. These findings identify how numerical choices can alter judgments of candidate restriction. Reporting candidate-pool stability and independently evaluated spread alongside reference agreement makes the basis of a measured quality--cost trade-off explicit.
new: Candidate restriction can reduce influence-maximization search costs, but evaluating its quality requires comparing two seed sets selected from finite samples. We vary the selection-world budget $W$ for both full-candidate and candidate-restricted greedy selection, separately from ranking precision, and evaluate spread on 10,000 independent worlds. Evidence comes from three external topologies, with four small contact graphs providing separate controls. On ca-GrQc, default PageRank-4k changes from 5.61\% higher to 5.07\% lower mean incremental spread relative to the same-budget full reference. This sign reversal disappears in a post-hoc control that tightens PageRank tolerance. Budget-dependent seed changes persist, but set changes alone do not determine the direction or magnitude of independently estimated spread changes. Across the external networks, degree-based pools reproduce all 15 highest-budget reference trajectories at lower measured selection cost, whereas PageRank losses persist on the two directed networks. These findings distinguish selection-budget sensitivity from candidate-ranking sensitivity. Reporting both selection procedures, candidate-pool stability and independently evaluated spread makes the basis of a measured quality--cost trade-off explicit.

old: Candidate-restriction quality must be interpreted relative to both a sampled reference and a numerically constructed candidate pool. Through paired controls and independent evaluation, this study separates numerical sensitivity, seed agreement and utility retention. On ca-GrQc, tightening PageRank tolerance removes the apparent budget-induced quality reversal, while budget-dependent seed changes remain. Across the external sample, Degree-4k preserves the tested $W=1280$ trajectories at lower measured selection cost, while PageRank outcomes depend on precision, coverage and network context. These findings make the basis of a measured quality--cost trade-off explicit. Their scope is the studied networks and settings; matching a finite reference does not establish expected-spread optimality. Joint precision--coupling controls and direction interventions are the next tests of the interpretation beyond the present comparisons.
new: Candidate-restriction quality depends on finite-world seed selection in both methods and on the ranking that defines the restricted pool. Increasing $W$ changes both selection procedures; independently evaluated relative differences therefore describe their joint response to the selection budget. On ca-GrQc, tightening PageRank tolerance removes the apparent budget-induced sign reversal, while budget-dependent seed changes remain. Separate reference-transition comparisons show that set changes can accompany positive, negative or zero estimated spread changes. Across the external sample, Degree-4k preserves the tested $W=1280$ trajectories at lower measured selection cost, whereas PageRank outcomes depend on precision, coverage and network context. Evaluation reports should distinguish the shared selection budget, the independent evaluation budget and candidate-pool construction, and report signed spread differences alongside scoped costs. These findings apply to the networks, propagation settings and implementations examined here.

At a fixed W, the post-hoc tolerance control recomputes the restricted arms and reuses the full reference selected at that budget.
